title: Economic Justice: An 8-Week Study
subtitle: A pastoral, even-handed five-session study that refuses both the preacher who blesses your portfolio and the politics that swallows the gospel, and keeps the cross at the center of money.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of money being preached as either a blessing to be claimed or a system to be torn down, and who want to know what Scripture actually says. It walks slowly through five essays by James Bell on what the Bible says about money, whether poverty is political, the economy God commanded in the Jubilee, the eye of the needle, and the difference between charity and justice. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

This is not a study that flatters one party and indicts the other. It catches both tribes. It asks the Christian who has reduced justice to a check written on Tuesday whether he has built himself a hiding place, and it asks the Christian who has reduced the gospel to a voting bloc whether he still believes the cross can accomplish anything without a majority. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has stretched toward security a thousand times and called it prudence, he holds notes and has expected return, he wears a shirt made by hands he will never meet. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: What the Bible Actually Says About Money
sessions.aim: To name money not as a neutral tool but as a power, a rival lord, and to refuse both the preacher who blesses wealth and the reader who reduces Scripture to anti-wealth politics.
sessions.summary: A man told Bell after a funeral that he had spent thirty years building something he could not take into the ground he was about to fill. He was not confessing greed. He was confessing surprise. The real question about money is not whether wealth is allowed but whether money is a neutral tool that takes its color from the user or a power that wants you. Scripture answers that it is a power, and it has a name, mammon. The spine is Paul to Timothy, that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils, a craving that reorganizes the whole interior around itself. Bell steel-mans the two answers that want to silence Paul. The prosperity teaching is right that God blesses, that creation is good, that the holiness of poverty is a Greek lie. But it cannot survive verse nine, where the desire to be rich is itself the trap. The secular reduction is right that the Bible is dangerous to the comfortable. But it cannot survive verse seventeen, where the rich are not abolished but commanded to bleed their wealth outward. Money is not neutral, which refutes the secular reading, and money is not safely blessed, which refutes the prosperity preacher. You cannot serve God and money. Not should not. Cannot. He who was rich became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich.

keyScripture.why: Jesus says you cannot serve God and money, naming mammon as a rival lord and describing a wiring that will not run two currents, not a rule but a description.

discussion.q: Bell says the real question is not whether wealth is allowed but whether money is a neutral tool or a power that wants you. Before tonight, which one did you assume it was?
discussion.behind: Surface the default before defining anything. Most people in the pew carry the tool assumption, that money is morally blank and only the user gives it color. The point is not to settle it yet but to show the assumption is there, unexamined. Land it on honesty, not consensus.

discussion.q: Paul does not say money is the root. He says the love of it is a root, a craving, a stretch toward. Where do you feel that stretch in your own week, and what costume does it wear?
discussion.behind: Push past the abstract. Bell says the stretch wears the costume of love and is sometimes only fear. You want people to name the actual reaching, the security dressed as prudence, the providing dressed as worship. If they cannot find it, that itself is the finding, because the most patient idol never asks for worship in words.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong form of the prosperity teaching, that creation is good and the holiness of poverty is a lie, before he answers it. What is true in it that you do not want to lose?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness from the start. The prosperity preacher is right that God made vineyards and oil and called them good, right that shame about the body has done damage. Make sure no one leaves thinking the answer is to despise material gifts. The error is not blessing. It is the craving bolted onto it.

discussion.q: He also takes the strong form of the secular reading, that the Bible is dangerous to the comfortable and means to be. Where has the comfortable version of your faith never been disturbed by money?
discussion.behind: Now turn the table the other way. The secular reader has actually read the prophets, which is more than many churchgoers can say. The aim is to let the indictment land on the comfortable believer, including the leader, without handing the gospel over to a class document. Hold both refutations in the same hand.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has stretched toward security a thousand times and dressed it as prudence, that the law indicts the writer before the reader. Where have you done the same?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to self-implication. You are not hunting for confession to shame anyone. You want each person, including you the leader, inside the indictment, because grace means nothing until the law has named you. Go first if the room is slow.

objections.objection: This is just shame about money dressed up as theology. God is a good Father who blesses His children, and all this suspicion of wealth is the old Greek lie that matter is dirty and spirit is clean.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true, because Bell grants it fully. Creation is good, God blesses, and the dualism that treats the field as filthy is a lie the church absorbed and never coughed up. Israel's God made vineyards and called them good. Then make the distinction gently. The warning is not against the gift but against the craving bolted onto it. Paul does not abolish wealth, he disarms it, commanding the rich to be rich in good works. You can receive blessing as a gift and still refuse to let the wanting become your master.

objections.objection: The Bible is obviously a class document. All this talk of the poor and the rich proves Christianity is just an ancient socialism, useful for guilt and nothing else.
objections.response: Grant what is right, because this reader has read the prophets when many have not. The Bible is not indifferent to who has and who lacks, and any Christianity that never disturbs the wealthy has not read its own book. Then press the other edge. Paul does not nationalize the vineyard, he haunts the man who owns it. That is not socialism, which seizes, and not capitalism, which absolves. The Bible names the rich man a debtor before God whose only hope is the same as the beggar's, a verdict no political menu has an item for.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the one thing you have quietly trusted money to deliver that, deep down, you suspect it cannot?
sessions.practice: This week, notice once when a money decision feels like a stretch toward security, and ask honestly whether it is love or fear wearing the costume of love. Do not fix it. Just name the temperature, and write down what it told you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we brought nothing into the world and we will take nothing out, and between those two empty hands we keep reaching for the one master who never asks for worship in words. You made the world good, and we have loved the gift in place of the giver. Show us the stretch in ourselves before it pierces us through. Free us from mammon, who will take us on any terms, and hold us to Christ, who has already paid for us in full. Amen.
reflection: Where have I dressed a craving for security in the language of prudence, and what would it cost me to call it by its real name?
Do I actually believe money is a power that wants me, or do I still treat it as a neutral tool I am safely in charge of?
If I traced my deepest trust on an ordinary anxious afternoon, would it run to God or to the strength I can point to in the bank?

sessions.title: Is Poverty Political? The Bible's Uncomfortable Answer
sessions.aim: To see that the prophets indict hearts and systems in the same breath, and to refuse both the privatized conscience and the politics that forgets the name of the poor man.
sessions.summary: Ask whether poverty is political in most American churches and faces close, because political has become a smell. So people answer fast. Poverty is a heart issue, they say, about generosity, not policy. Bell shared the instinct, and then he read Amos. The real question is whether the command to care for the poor speaks only to private compassion or also to the systems compassion operates inside. The prophets do not let us choose. Amos attacks a transaction, a courtroom verdict bought with silver, the selling of the needy for a pair of sandals. That is a political charge in any century. Bell steel-mans the conservative instinct, that making poverty political swaps the costly personal work of love for the cheap absolution of a vote, that a man who marches for the poor and never opens his door has learned to love humanity to avoid loving a human. The warning is true. But it cannot be the whole answer, because the same prophets spend most of their breath on structures, false balances, the joining of house to house, the gleaning law that builds provision into the field. The word is mishpat, the active intervention that puts wrong things right, joined to tsedaqah, right relationship lived out. Then the reversal. The man who insists poverty is only a heart issue has built the perfect hiding place, handing bread on Tuesday and voting Wednesday to keep the court rigged. The cross is where God's mishpat and mercy meet in a single act.

keyScripture.why: Amos indicts not a feeling but a transaction, the righteous sold for silver and the needy for sandals, naming a rigged court as the sin and making poverty a structural charge.

discussion.q: Bell says the word political has become a smell in church, a signal someone is about to import the news cycle into the sanctuary. Why does that instinct run so strong, and what does it protect us from?
discussion.behind: Open on the reflex itself, not on policy. The instinct keeps the gospel from being captured by a party, which is a real good. But it can also quietly excuse us from a whole half of what the prophets say. Help the room see the instinct is reasonable and incomplete before anyone defends a position.

discussion.q: Amos does not attack a feeling. He attacks a courtroom verdict bought with silver. What changes when you notice the prophet is preaching against a rigged court and not against stinginess at the dinner table?
discussion.behind: You want the concrete shift. Amos names weights and measures, the consolidation of land, the architecture of an ancient economy. The aim is the recognition that Scripture indicts structures and not only hearts, so that keeping faith private is not the neutral biblical default it feels like.

discussion.q: Christopher Wright and Tim Keller say mishpat and tsedaqah cannot be pried apart, that to have private piety without doing justice is to be privately clean and publicly complicit. Where do you feel that tension in your own life?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. The Bible has no category for a righteous person content to live inside an unjust arrangement. Do not let this become a policy debate. Keep it on the personal recognition that mercy felt and justice done are two different verbs, and we trade the second away.

discussion.q: Bell takes the conservative warning seriously, that a man can love humanity in the abstract to avoid loving a human, that government compassion can be compassion with someone else's hands. What is true in that warning that we must keep?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness deliberately here. The warning against substituting the system for the soul is true. Make sure participants who fear politicized faith feel honored, not dismissed, before the reversal lands. Bell grants the whole of it before he turns it.

discussion.q: Then he turns it. The man who insists poverty is only a heart issue can feed the poor on Tuesday and vote Wednesday to keep the gate rigged, and feel clean both days. Where might that hiding place be in you?
discussion.behind: Close the loop with self-implication. Bell says the shirt he is wearing was made by hands he will never meet under conditions he would not accept for his sons, that he is implicated before he has done one cruel thing. Invite gentle, non-defensive recognition, and go first.

objections.objection: When you make poverty political you replace the slow, costly, personal work of love with the cheap satisfaction of voting for a program and feeling absolved. The early church did not lobby Caesar, it sold its possessions and laid them at the apostles' feet.
objections.response: Bell preaches this himself, so grant it with full weight. A man who marches for the poor and never opens his door has learned to love humanity in order to avoid loving a human, and charity that becomes only policy does rot into a transaction between strangers. The warning against substituting the system for the soul is true. Then add the half it misses. The same prophets who indict greed spend most of their breath on weights, measures, and land, and the gleaning law structures the field whether the owner feels charitable or not. Personal love is required. It was never meant to excuse us from asking who built the gate.

objections.objection: Faith is about the inner man. Keep the government out of the gospel and let the church change hearts, and the structures will take care of themselves.
objections.response: Treat this gently, because it sounds like humility. But Bell shows it is not the neutral position it pretends to be. Charles Taylor traced how the modern order invited religion in as private motivation but not public claim, and the church mostly took the bargain, kept the inner life, and handed the structures to the market and the state. We called that humility. It was abdication. The God who broke an empire to free His slaves audits the city as well as the heart, and a faith with nothing to say to Pharaoh is not the faith of the Exodus.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who is the poor man at your own gate whose name you have never actually learned, and what has the not-learning protected you from?
sessions.practice: This week, choose one thing you give to or feel good about, and trace it back one step. Ask who built the arrangement the need grows out of, and whether your part is feeling kindness or doing justice. Write down what you find, and let it be uncomfortable.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you search my heart and you also audit my city, and you have never once agreed to inspect the one and ignore the other. Forgive us for keeping our compassion safely indoors and calling it humility. Forgive the hiding places we have built, the bread we hand with one hand while the other keeps the gate rigged. Teach us to do justice and not only to feel it, and send us back to the gate with the name of the poor man on our lips. Amen.
reflection: Where have I treated keeping faith private as the safe, neutral position, when it was actually a way to avoid the cost of justice?
Have I ever let the warmth of charity stand in for the harder work of doing justice, and how would I know the difference if I looked?
What arrangement do I benefit from that I did not build, and what does honesty about that benefit ask of me this week?

sessions.title: Jubilee, Debt, and the Economy God Commanded
sessions.aim: To take the Jubilee as a real economic command and not a spiritualized antique, and to hear in our certainty that it is impractical the confession of the bondage it was given to break.
sessions.summary: There is a law in Leviticus so strange most Christians have never heard it preached. Every fiftieth year a trumpet sounds on the Day of Atonement and the whole economy resets. Land returns. Debts dissolve. Those who sold themselves to survive a bad harvest walk free. God built into the calendar a recurring undoing of accumulation, and the church has spent two thousand years finding reasons He could not have meant it. The question is whether Jubilee is a spiritualized antique or a command with teeth. Bell gives the strong case for the dismissal. There is little evidence Israel practiced it nationally, it belongs to a vanished agrarian world, and the New Testament fills the language with spiritual content when Jesus reads Isaiah at Nazareth. Bell grants that Jubilee points past itself, that Jesus fills deror with a depth no land transfer could hold, that we cannot drop bronze-age statutes unaltered into a world of mortgages. But the dismissal converts the fact that Jubilee points beyond economics into the claim it was never about economics at all, and that is evasion dressed as exegesis. The text regulates the sale price by counting harvests. You cannot spiritualize a pricing formula. The reason debts release is that the land is mine, says the Lord, and they were tenants. Then the reversal. We say Jubilee is impractical because our system runs on permanent compounding debt, which is precisely the bondage Jubilee was given to break.

keyScripture.why: The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine, naming all ownership as tenancy under God and making property real but penultimate, held and not finally possessed.

discussion.q: God built a recurring undoing of accumulation into the calendar and called it Jubilee. What is your first reaction to a God who legislates the cancellation of debt, and where does that reaction come from?
discussion.behind: Open on the gut response before the arguments. Many will feel it cannot be serious, which is exactly the instinct Bell wants to examine. The point is to surface our resistance to the plain claim of the text so we can ask later whether the resistance is exegesis or evasion.

discussion.q: Bell grants the strongest dismissal, that Jubilee points past itself to the soul's release in Christ. He grants it and then says the dismissal goes one step too far. What is the step too far?
discussion.behind: You want the precise move named. It is true Jubilee points beyond economics. The evasion is converting that into the claim it was never about economics at all. The text prices land by counting harvests. Help the room see you can honor the spiritual depth without erasing the concrete command.

discussion.q: The reason debts release is one sentence, the land is mine, you are tenants. How does it change the way you hold what you own to hear that you never finally owned it?
discussion.behind: This is the theological center. Property is real but penultimate, held in trust, not absolute. Do not let it drift into abstraction. Press on actual deeds, savings, and grip. The conviction that ultimate ownership belongs to God is the foundation the dismissal must bury to keep Jubilee in the past.

discussion.q: Bell says when we call Jubilee unrealistic we are not arguing against it, we are confessing the bondage it was meant to break, a system that runs on permanent compounding debt. Does that reversal land, or do you want to resist it?
discussion.behind: Let people push back honestly. The reversal is strong but it can be overstated. The aim is not to produce a policy but to feel the diagnosis, that the impracticality of release is itself a symptom of a machine that requires the farmer never get his land back. Keep prudential policy and biblical conviction distinct.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he holds notes, that he has lent and expected return, that the law of Jubilee indicts the lender in him. Where does this law indict you, and what do you not want to loosen your grip on?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. Bell does not stand outside the lender. Invite people to name the thing they would be slow to release, the debt they are owed, the field they have accumulated. Go first. The point is honesty before the grace of the One who became the Jubilee Israel never kept.

objections.objection: Jubilee was always pointing past itself to spiritual release. Jesus proclaims liberty from sin, not land redistribution. To literalize it is to miss the gospel for the economics.
objections.response: Bell agrees Jubilee points past itself, that Jesus fills deror with a depth no land transfer could hold, and that the captivity He breaks is older than debt. Grant all of it. Then name the overreach. The dismissal slides from Jubilee points beyond economics to Jubilee was never about economics, and the text will not allow it. It regulates the sale price by counting harvests until the next release. You cannot spiritualize a pricing formula. The release of the captive and the release of the debtor were never two things. They were the same mercy at two depths.

objections.objection: Then the answer is to legislate Leviticus 25 today, cancel the debts, redistribute the land, and build the Jubilee economy into law right now.
objections.response: Bell rules this out as firmly as the spiritualizing. We cannot lift bronze-age agrarian statutes and drop them unmodified into a world of mortgages and sovereign bonds, and anyone who reads Leviticus 25 as a ready-made fiscal bill has understood neither Leviticus nor fiscal policy. Jubilee is not a spreadsheet. The command is real and the application is prudential, and confusing the two cheapens both. What it asks is whether we will live as tenants and not owners, whether we will loosen our grip on the field while we still can, not whether we can pass it as a budget line.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you truly held everything you own as a tenant and not an owner, what is the first thing your hands would loosen?
sessions.practice: This week, find one debt you are owed, financial or otherwise, and one thing you have accumulated and gripped. Ask before God whether you could release the one and loosen the other, and write down what rises up in you when you imagine doing it.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of the trumpet and the Day of Atonement, You set the release of debts on the same day You set the release of guilt, because in Your economy they were always the same act. We have learned to want the second and refuse the first. Remind us we are strangers and sojourners with You, holding deeds that were never absolute, on ground that was never finally ours. Make us willing to live as if that is true. In the name of Jesus, who is the Jubilee we never kept, amen.
reflection: What have I treated as absolutely mine that Scripture says I only ever held as a tenant under God?
When I call the Jubilee impractical, am I making an argument against it, or confessing the bondage it was given to break?
Is there a debt I am owed or a thing I have accumulated that God may be asking me to release while I still can?

sessions.title: The Eye of the Needle: Jesus and the Rich
sessions.aim: To let Jesus mean the impossibility He spoke, refusing the invented gate that softens it, and to hear the disciples' despair as the door through which the gospel reaches us.
sessions.summary: A story got told of a low gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye, through which a camel could squeeze if you unloaded its cargo and made it kneel. The point was relief. The rich man can get in after all. It is a fabrication, with no evidence before the Middle Ages, invented to relieve a pressure the church could not bear. Jesus meant the largest animal and the smallest hole. He meant it cannot be done. The real question is why we needed the gate. The answer is that we are the rich man and we would rather believe in a fictional gate than face a real impossibility. The spine is the rich young ruler who runs, kneels, has kept the commandments from his youth, and is loved by Jesus, who tells him to sell all and follow, and who walks away sorrowful. Bell gives the strong softening reading, that Jesus diagnoses this man's particular idol, that Zacchaeus kept half and was saved, that the saying is about whatever you grip. It is partly right. But Jesus names the category, those who have wealth, not the heart-condition in the abstract, and when the disciples ask who then can be saved He widens the impossibility rather than easing it. Wealth is the idol that does not feel like one, hiding inside prudence and responsibility and love of family. Then the reversal. The disciples despair, and the despair is correct. With man it is impossible is not the bad news before the gospel. It is the gospel's first word of truth.

keyScripture.why: Jesus says it is easier for a camel to pass through a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom, driving the saying past difficulty into impossibility and refusing to let it be managed.

discussion.q: The church forged an architectural feature, a gate that never existed, to escape this sentence. Why does the plain sense of the eye of the needle frighten us so badly that we would invent a way around it?
discussion.behind: Open on the fear, not the exegesis. Bell says we are the rich man and we know it. The aim is to let the room feel the pressure the invented gate was built to release, so that the rest of the session has somewhere to land. Do not solve it yet. Sit in why we needed an exit.

discussion.q: Bell takes the gentle reading seriously, that Jesus diagnosed this man's particular idol and that Zacchaeus kept half and was saved. What is true in that reading, and what does it have to ignore to stay gentle?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. Jesus does tailor commands and wealth is not the only idol. But the gentle reading must ignore that Jesus names the category, those who have wealth, and that He widens the impossibility when the disciples ask who can be saved. Help them feel the saying being managed and then refusing to be.

discussion.q: Bell says wealth is the idol that does not feel like one, hiding inside security, prudence, responsibility, love of family. Where has money hidden inside a virtue in your own life?
discussion.behind: This is the heart of the session. The man who worships success feels his hunger, but wealth presents itself as care for one's family. Press on the disguise. The camel cannot fit because it cannot imagine it needs to, its size invisible to itself. Invite people to find the place their grip wears the costume of duty.

discussion.q: Tim Keller says we have become expert at applying every hard saying about money to someone richer than ourselves, the rich man always the next bracket up. When you read this, who did you picture, and was it ever you?
discussion.behind: Even-handed and convicting at once. Bell notes we who are richer than the ruler ever dreamed still aim the saying upward. The gate moved from the wall into our hermeneutics, built now out of exegesis. The aim is the recognition that the rich man in the story is the one in the pew, including the leader.

discussion.q: The disciples respond with despair, asking who then can be saved, and Bell says the despair is the right response. Why is being crushed by this saying the door rather than the dead end?
discussion.behind: Close on the reversal. The objection that the saying is too harsh is not a problem to be solved, it is the door. The moment you stop trying to thread the camel by your own management and confess it cannot be done, you are where the gospel can reach you. With man it is impossible is the first word of truth, not the bad news before grace.

objections.objection: Jesus did not mean wealth as such. He diagnosed this one man's idol. Zacchaeus and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and welcomed, so the saying is really about whatever you grip, not money.
objections.response: Bell grants the partial truth. Jesus does diagnose individuals, He did love this man and tailor the command, and wealth is not the only idol. But the gentle reading has to ignore that Jesus names the category, those who have wealth, and that when the disciples ask who can be saved He widens the impossibility instead of softening it. Wealth is the idol that does not feel like one, hiding inside prudence and love of family. The softening turns the saying into a manageable warning. Jesus drives it past difficulty into impossibility and leaves it there on purpose.

objections.objection: If no rich person can be saved on these terms, then the saying is simply too harsh to be true, and we should not take it at face value.
objections.response: This is not a problem to be solved. It is the door. The disciples felt exactly this, were exceedingly astonished, and asked who then can be saved, and their despair was correct. The saying is meant to crush, to take the best man in the room, the one who kept the commandments from his youth, and show him he cannot purchase his way in by obedience any more than by money. The harshness drives you to stop managing the camel and confess it cannot be done, and that confession is where the One for whom all things are possible finally reaches you.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the possession or security you would be slowest to sell, even to follow the One you say you follow?
sessions.practice: This week, when a money decision presents itself as simple prudence or responsibility, pause and ask whether the virtue is hiding an idol. Do not rush to sell anything. Just let the saying measure you, and write down what it shows you about your own grip.
sessions.closingPrayer: Jesus, You said it is impossible, and we have spent centuries building gates to escape what You meant. We are the camel, too large and too laden, too sure of our own keeping. Stop us from threading ourselves through by management. Let the saying take our breath the way it took the disciples', and then turn our despair into the door, so that having stopped trying to fit, we let ourselves be carried through the needle You alone could pass. Amen.
reflection: Where have I aimed every hard saying about money at someone richer than me, so that the rich man in the story is never the man I see in the mirror?
What virtue, prudence or responsibility or love of family, has a grip on possessions been hiding inside of?
Have I let the impossibility of this saying crush me into despair, or have I kept building a gate so I never have to stop and be carried?

sessions.title: Charity Is Not Justice: The Difference That Changes Everything
sessions.aim: To distinguish doing justice from loving kindness in Micah's two verbs, and to see how charity, when it refuses justice, installs the giver as a small lord over a wound he has agreed to keep.
sessions.summary: There is a generosity that costs the giver nothing he cannot spare and changes nothing he does not wish to change. We have perfected it. We write the check, serve the meal, and go home undisturbed, because the arrangement that produced the hungry man is as intact in the evening as in the morning. Bell has done this, has felt the warm relief of having given and mistaken it for righteousness. The real question is whether charity and justice are the same impulse at different sizes, so that enough charity adds up to justice, or different things entirely, so that charity can become the enemy of justice by relieving the pressure justice requires. The spine is Micah, do justice, and love kindness, and walk humbly. Two verbs govern two things. You do justice, mishpat, and you love kindness, chesed. Micah holds them apart on purpose, because you can love kindness and still refuse to do justice. Bell steel-mans charity, that justice is slow and the man at the gate is hungry tonight, that charity is personal and humble where the activist is tempted to play God. He grants it fully. Chesed is commanded. But charity without justice becomes a way of managing a wound we have decided to keep. The gleaning law builds provision into the field as the poor man's entitlement, not the owner's mood. Then the reversal. The charity that refuses justice installs the giver as a small lord, and justice dethrones him. The cross is mishpat and chesed no longer pried apart, the debt honored and the debtor forgiven in one death.

keyScripture.why: Two verbs govern two things, to do justice and to love kindness, and Micah holds them apart so the warm feeling of mercy can never be swapped for the costly work of justice.

discussion.q: Bell admits he has felt the warm relief of having given and mistaken the relief for righteousness. Have you felt that relief, and what did it let you stop thinking about?
discussion.behind: Open with honesty and self-implication together. The warm relief is real and not evil, but it can close the question. The aim is to name the feeling without shaming the giving, so the room can later ask what the relief quietly excused them from. Go first as the leader.

discussion.q: Micah uses two different verbs, do justice and love kindness. Why does it matter that justice is something you do and kindness is something you love, and what trade does keeping them separate prevent?
discussion.behind: You want the grammar felt. The English flattens it, but Micah blocked the trade in the words. You can love kindness, feel the warm pull of mercy, and still refuse to do justice. The point is that the two are not the same size of one thing, and the one cannot be swapped for the other.

discussion.q: The gleaning law does not tell the owner to harvest everything and then give some away. It tells him not to reap the edges at all, so the poor gather what God assigned them as a right. What changes when provision is an entitlement and not a gift?
discussion.behind: This is the concrete center. Christopher Wright says the gleaning laws make provision a matter of the poor man's entitlement under God, not the owner's generosity, and the difference is the difference between justice and charity. The poor man does not depend on the landowner's mood. Help them feel the dignity the structure protects.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case for charity, that it feeds the hungry tonight while the theorists argue, that it is personal and humble where the activist risks playing God. What is true in that case that you do not want to lose?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness firmly. Any argument that makes a man ashamed of feeding the hungry has gone wrong. Chesed is commanded, the danger is never that we are too merciful. Make sure those who love the soup kitchen feel honored before the reversal lands. Bell grants it fully and means it.

discussion.q: Then he turns it. What is more godlike, Bell asks, than to stand permanently above the poor man as his benefactor, the one with the power to give or withhold? Where might your charity be installing you as a small lord?
discussion.behind: Close on the reversal and the self-implication. Charity that refuses justice makes the giver a small lord, and justice dethrones him by saying the poor man was owed all along. Bell says he has lived off fields harvested to the edge and called the leftovers charity. Invite gentle recognition, not defensiveness, and stand in it yourself.

objections.objection: Justice is slow, abstract, and contested, but the man at the gate is hungry tonight, and charity feeds him tonight. Do not sneer at the soup kitchen. It has fed more real bodies than every theory of justice combined.
objections.response: Bell grants this fully and refuses to win cheaply. Charity is good, chesed is commanded, the prophet says love it, and any argument that shames a man for feeding the hungry has gone wrong. The danger is never that we are too merciful. Then hear the distinction. The point is not that charity is bad and justice good, but that charity without justice becomes a way of managing a wound we have decided to keep. Niebuhr saw that private benevolence can let the powerful feel virtuous while the structures of their power stay untouched. Feed the man tonight. Do not let the feeding become the reason you never ask why he is at the gate.

objections.objection: All this talk of structural justice just makes the activist into someone who loves humanity in the abstract and plays God with everyone else's lives. The humble path is personal charity, not grand schemes of justice.
objections.response: Turn it over, because the humility runs the other way. What is more presumptuous than to stand permanently above the poor man as his benefactor, the one whose generosity he must depend on and be grateful for? Charity that refuses justice installs the giver as a small lord. Justice dethrones him by saying the poor man has a claim that does not run through your goodwill, an entitlement under God you must honor whether you feel charitable or not. The humble position is not remaining the gracious giver forever. It is admitting the man at the gate was owed something all along.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you give, do you want to remain the gracious benefactor, or are you willing to admit the person was owed something that was never yours to grant?
sessions.practice: This week, take one act of giving you already do and ask Micah's two questions of it. What can I spare for the man at the gate, and who built the gate and what is he owed. Do both verbs, love the kindness and begin to do the justice, and write down where the second one costs you more than the first.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, You told us plainly what is good, to do justice and to love kindness and to walk humbly with You, and we have traded the first verb away and kept the safe one. Forgive us for becoming generous managers of wounds we agreed to keep open, for the small lordship we mistook for mercy. On the cross You entered the field and paid the debt of justice we owed, mishpat and chesed in one death. Send us back to do justice and not only to feel it. Amen.
reflection: Where have I let the warm feeling of charity stand in for the costly work of justice, and what has that trade let me avoid?
Has my generosity ever made me a small lord, the benefactor whose goodwill the poor must depend on, rather than one who honors what they were owed?
If I asked of my giving both of Micah's verbs, what would change about how, and to whom, and why I give?

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here. Before we start, three things. First, this study was written to indict every tribe, including mine and yours, so we are not here to score points against the people who are not in the room, the ones who reduce justice to a check or the ones who reduce the gospel to a vote. Second, nobody has to perform certainty. You can be unsure out loud, and you can change your mind. Third, the writer puts himself inside everything he says, and so will we. He holds notes, he has stretched toward security and called it prudence, he wears a shirt made by hands he will never meet. We are not pointing from a safe distance. We are standing in it. Tonight we are looking at this theme together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the essay says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the week we are about to walk into, because none of this matters if it stays an idea about other people's money.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not resolved, because Bell does not resolve it either and neither should we. Take the weight of this out with you rather than setting it down at the door. Try the practice this week. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And come back ready to be honest, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go, and then I will see you next time. Thank you for the courage it took to be in this conversation.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set ground rules, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, What the Bible Actually Says About Money, full discussion and practice.
Week 3: Session 2, Is Poverty Political, with extended time on mishpat and tsedaqah.
Week 4: Session 3, Jubilee, Debt, and the Economy God Commanded.
Week 5: Session 4, The Eye of the Needle, part one through the rich young ruler and the camel saying.
Week 6: Session 4 continued, the disciples' despair and the impossibility as the door, plus practice.
Week 7: Session 5, Charity Is Not Justice.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and what each person is carrying out.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, money as a power and the question of whether poverty is political.
Week 2: Session 3, Jubilee, with extended time on the land is mine and tenancy under God.
Week 3: Session 4, The Eye of the Needle, the impossibility and the door.
Week 4: Session 5, Charity Is Not Justice, plus a short integration close.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, What the Bible Actually Says About Money.
Week 2: Session 2, Is Poverty Political, The Bible's Uncomfortable Answer.
Week 3: Session 3, Jubilee, Debt, and the Economy God Commanded.
Week 4: Session 4, The Eye of the Needle, Jesus and the Rich.
Week 5: Session 5, Charity Is Not Justice, The Difference That Changes Everything.

bibliography.title: Generous Justice: How God's Grace Makes Us Just
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Where Keller shows that mishpat and tsedaqah cannot be pried apart, that private piety without public justice is complicity. The pastoral spine of sessions 2 and 5.

bibliography.title: Counterfeit Gods: The Empty Promises of Money, Sex, and Power
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Source of the observation that we apply every hard saying about money to someone richer than ourselves, the rich man always the next bracket up. Anchors session 4.

bibliography.title: Old Testament Ethics for the People of God
bibliography.author: Christopher J. H. Wright
bibliography.note: Defines mishpat as the active intervention that puts wrong things right and shows the gleaning laws make provision an entitlement, not a favor. Central to sessions 2, 3, and 5.

bibliography.title: The Prophetic Imagination
bibliography.author: Walter Brueggemann
bibliography.note: Traces the royal consciousness of Solomon's economy of accumulation and the prophets who rose as the alternative consciousness of the God of the Exodus. Grounds the history in session 2.

bibliography.title: Sin: A History
bibliography.author: Gary A. Anderson
bibliography.note: Shows how sin came to be pictured as a debt and almsgiving as paying it down, so that financial and moral debt were never separate in the Hebrew mind. Background for sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: Money and Power
bibliography.author: Jacques Ellul
bibliography.note: Argues money is not a tool we picked up but a power we serve, and the pretense that it is neutral is the lie that lets it rule. Anchors session 1.

bibliography.title: A Secular Age
bibliography.author: Charles Taylor
bibliography.note: Traces how the modern order came to imagine itself as a self-running economic mechanism, removing the moral question from the center of economic life to the edges. Used in sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: Home Economics
bibliography.author: Wendell Berry
bibliography.note: Argues that an economy which treats the love of gain as harmless will treat the land, the neighbor, and the body as raw material for it. Supports session 1's account of accumulation.

bibliography.title: On Wealth and Poverty
bibliography.author: John Chrysostom
bibliography.note: The fourth-century homilies that call the rich man who hoards what the poor need a kind of thief, withholding what is not finally his. Cited in sessions 1 and 4.

bibliography.title: Moral Man and Immoral Society: A Study in Ethics and Politics
bibliography.author: Reinhold Niebuhr
bibliography.note: Where Niebuhr argues private benevolence can become a substitute for and an obstacle to justice, salving the conscience justice would convict. Central to session 5.

bibliography.title: The Biblical Vision of Sabbath Economics
bibliography.author: Ched Myers
bibliography.note: Connects the Sabbath-Jubilee tradition from the manna in the wilderness to the early Jerusalem church holding all things in common. Supports session 3. Leader to confirm the specifics before pressing them as settled history.

bibliography.title: Neither Poverty Nor Riches: A Biblical Theology of Possessions
bibliography.author: Craig Blomberg
bibliography.note: A careful survey holding together the Bible's affirmation of material goods and its severe warnings about wealth, refusing both poles. Not cited by Bell directly. Leader to confirm before attributing any specific claim to it, useful as a balancing voice across all five sessions.

bibliography.title: Rich Christians in an Age of Hunger
bibliography.author: Ron Sider
bibliography.note: A widely read evangelical call to costly generosity and structural concern for the poor. Not cited by Bell directly and contested by some readers. Leader to confirm before stating its arguments as the study's position, offered as one influential voice for session 5.

bibliography.title: What Is the Mission of the Church?
bibliography.author: Kevin DeYoung and Greg Gilbert
bibliography.note: Presses the case that the church's central mission is the proclamation of the gospel and warns against collapsing mission into social and economic action. Offered as the counterweight for the even-handedness of session 2. Leader to confirm before stating its arguments as Bell's own.

furtherReading: Generous Justice, Timothy Keller, for readers who want the fuller pastoral case behind sessions 2 and 5 that grace makes the forgiven just.
Old Testament Ethics for the People of God, Christopher Wright, for those who want to think harder about mishpat, gleaning, and the economy of the Torah.
Neither Poverty Nor Riches, Craig Blomberg, for a balanced biblical theology of possessions that refuses both the prosperity pole and the anti-wealth pole, leader to confirm specific claims.

What Is the Mission of the Church, Kevin DeYoung and Greg Gilbert, for readers who want the strongest case that the church's first task is the gospel and not economic reform, read alongside the study's affirmation of justice.
On Wealth and Poverty, John Chrysostom, for those willing to hear the ancient ferocity about hoarding that we have softened into a stewardship seminar.

glossary.definition: The Aramaic word Jesus personifies as a rival lord, a god with a small g that asks not for worship in words but for your trust, a little more each year. Not money as such, but money treated as a master.

The Hebrew word usually rendered justice, but not the blind even-handedness of a Western courtroom. It is the active intervention that puts wrong things right and takes the side of the one who cannot defend himself, the widow, the orphan, the stranger, the poor.

Hebrew for righteousness, but not private moral cleanness. It is right relationship lived out in the community's economic life, so generous and so structurally fair that it cannot be pried apart from mishpat.
Covenant mercy, faithful love, the kindness Micah says we are to love. It is real and commanded, but it is the verb we are tempted to swap for the harder verb of doing justice.

The law of Leviticus 25 commanding that every fiftieth year the land return to the family that lost it, debts dissolve, and servants go free. A recurring, legislated undoing of accumulation, sounded on the Day of Atonement.

The Hebrew word for liberty proclaimed in the Jubilee, the same word Isaiah's anointed one uses and Jesus reads at Nazareth, binding the release of the debtor and the release of the captive into one mercy at two depths.

The Torah command not to reap the field to its edges, so the poor and the sojourner could gather what God assigned them as a right. It builds provision for the poor into the structure of the field rather than the owner's mood.

The lending of money at interest, forbidden by the church for over a thousand years on the ground that money is barren and time is not ours to sell. The prohibition cracked in the sixteenth century under the pressure of commerce, not refutation.

The theological idea that God gives genuine gifts, order, beauty, and justice, to all people and societies, believing or not, which lets Christians honor real good in their economy without worshiping wealth or treating the field as filthy.

Sin lodged not only in individual hearts but in arrangements, courts, weights, measures, and laws, so that a person can benefit from injustice without committing one cruel act. The prophets indict it alongside personal sin in the same breath.
Sin in the individual heart and act, greed, dishonesty, the stretch toward security dressed as prudence. Scripture refuses to let it be split from structural sin, naming both at once.

The view that God means to bless His people with material abundance and that faith claims it. Right that creation is good and poverty is not holy, but it bolts a craving onto blessing and baptizes the very reaching Paul called a root of evils.

Almsgiving from giver to receiver, good and commanded as chesed, but when it refuses justice it becomes a way of managing a wound we have decided to keep, installing the giver as a small lord over the poor man's dependence.

Brueggemann's name for the economy of accumulation, managed abundance, and forced labor that Solomon built, against which the prophets rose as the alternative consciousness remembering the God who broke the economy of Pharaoh's bricks.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Money gets preached two ways, as a blessing to claim or a system to tear down, and almost nobody stops to ask what Scripture actually says. This five-session study walks slowly through money as a power, whether poverty is political, the economy God commanded in the Jubilee, the eye of the needle, and the difference between charity and justice. It is even-handed, catching the Christian who reduces justice to a check and the one who reduces the gospel to a vote, and it implicates all of us. Built so any volunteer can lead it with no prep. Join us as we keep the cross at the center of money.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We are starting a five-week study on economic justice, and before anyone braces, hear this. It is not a stewardship seminar and it is not a partisan study. It catches both tribes, the one that reduces justice to private charity and the one that reduces the gospel to politics, and it implicates the preacher first. It asks the hard, simple question of who serves whom when it comes to money. No homework, and no prep needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: Money keeps its promises and breaks them in the same motion. It delivers the house. It does not deliver the man who can live in it. A five-session study on what the Bible actually says about money, even-handed enough to catch every tribe and honest enough to start with the leader. Come honest, not finished.
